lines: Jamie Alvarez
+1 (555) 010-5820 | jamie.alvarez@example.com | example.com/in/jalvarez
EDUCATION
Riverbend Polytechnic | B.S. in Industrial Engineering | Metro City, USA | Sep 2014 - May 2018
EXPERIENCE
Greenleaf Florist | Delivery Driver and Shop Assistant | Metro City, USA | Sep 2025 - Present
- Delivered 30 to 40 arrangements a day across the city and took cash and card payments at the door.
- Prepared weekend wedding orders with the head florist and kept the cooler stocked and labeled.
Lakeview Distribution | Operations Analyst | Metro City, USA | Jul 2018 - Jan 2021
- Raised forecast accuracy from 70% to 85% by switching the MAPE calculation to cover only SKUs that sold every week.
- Ran a time study of the returns desk; my findings led to a triage station that cut returns processing time from 3 days to 1.
- Wrote the dock scheduling rules for 12 carriers, cutting average trailer wait at the dock from 95 to 40 minutes.
- Set up cycle counting for the 2,000 highest-value locations, raising inventory record accuracy from 91% to 98.5% within a year.
Crestway Foods | Supply Chain Planner | Metro City, USA | Feb 2021 - Jul 2025
- Rebuilt weekly demand planning for 1,400 SKUs across 3 distribution centers with a seasonal forecast model, cutting stockouts from 6.2% to 2.8% while inventory fell by $1.9M.
- Cut inbound freight cost per pallet from $48 to $41 over two quarters by consolidating supplier pickups into four regional milk runs.
- Set reorder points for every SKU from 18 months of daily demand and supplier lead-time data, reviewed monthly with the category managers.

- Scoring 40 vendors weekly on on-time delivery, fill rate, lead-time variance and invoice accuracy, and sharing the scorecards with buyers before each quarterly review, raised on-time inbound deliveries from 81% to 93%.
- Raised the packaging line's overall equipment effectiveness (OEE) from 71% to 112% by cutting changeover time and micro-stops.
- Trained 6 planners on the new forecasting workflow and wrote its exception-handling guide, which the team still uses for promotions.
PROJECTS
Last-Mile Routing Study | Independent Project | Python | Oct 2024 - Present
- Modeled a regional grocer's 85 daily delivery stops as a vehicle-routing problem, cutting planned route miles 18% against the grocer's current routes.
- Cut average route length from 120 to 90 miles, a 40% reduction, by solving the routing problem with customer time windows.
- Raised on-time deliveries by 9% in simulation, from 84% to 93%, by adding customer time windows to the routing model.
Regional Food Bank Warehouse | Volunteer Consultant, Team of 4 | Excel | Mar 2022 - Jul 2022
- Analyzed warehouse operations and made recommendations to the food bank's leadership.
- The donation intake process was mapped and two duplicate data-entry steps were removed, so donations reached the shelves a day sooner.
- Wrote a slotting guide that the volunteer coordinators used to re-slot the warehouse again after its spring expansion.
SKILLS
Tools: Excel, Python
Methods: demand forecasting, inventory planning, time studies, vehicle routing

items.says: Experience is not listed newest-first: Lakeview appears above the more recent Crestway role.
items.because: Recruiters expect the most recent professional experience first, and the current order delays the latest relevant supply-chain work.

items.says: Education appears before seven years of professional experience.
items.because: The degree receives disproportionate prominence over recent accomplishments and career progression.

items.says: The prominent Greenleaf entry makes the career direction appear to move backward from operations and supply chain work.
items.because: Its placement and two bullets give it more visual weight than the relevant roles without explaining the transition.

items.says: The Last-Mile Routing Study is separated from the supply-chain experience it reinforces and is less prominent than the florist role.
items.because: Its placement makes relevant routing, simulation, and Python evidence harder to connect with the professional record.

items.says: The delivery count shows workload but not the result or value of the deliveries.
items.because: The reader cannot tell whether deliveries were timely, accurate, reliable, or otherwise successful.

items.says: The wedding-order and cooler duties do not show what they achieved.
items.because: Without an outcome, the line reads as routine responsibilities rather than evidence of contribution.

items.says: “Prepared weekend wedding orders” does not identify what preparation the candidate personally performed.
items.because: The broad wording makes the candidate's practical skill and responsibility difficult to assess.

items.says: The claimed rise in forecast accuracy from 70% to 85% is invalid because the MAPE calculation changed to cover only weekly-selling SKUs.
items.because: Changing the SKU population makes the figures non-comparable and can improve the reported metric without improving forecasting performance.

items.says: “My findings” uses a first-person pronoun, and the candidate's role in creating the triage station is unclear.
items.because: The pronoun breaks the impersonal style, while the causal wording does not distinguish informing, designing, or implementing the station.

items.says: The processing-time figures do not identify what summary of processing time they represent.
The processing-time result appears only after the study and station description.
items.because: This slows recognition of the strongest evidence.

items.says: The trailer-wait reduction is buried after the scheduling rules and carrier count.
“Set up” is generic, and the inventory-accuracy improvement follows the process description.
The reorder-points bullet states the task and scale but not what changed as a result.
items.because: The reader cannot tell whether it reduced stockouts, excess inventory, planner effort, or another problem.

items.says: “From 18 months of daily demand and supplier lead-time data” makes the source of the reorder points less clear than “using” that data.
The vendor-scorecard result is delayed by a participial opening, four measures, and two timing clauses.
The claim that OEE rose to 112% is invalid under the standard OEE definition, and the line does not establish what 112% measures.
items.because: Standard OEE cannot exceed 100%, so the figure indicates a calculation, denominator, or metric-definition error.

items.says: “Cutting changeover time and micro-stops” names loss categories rather than the actions that delivered the improvement.
Continued use of the guide shows adoption but not what it improved.
The 18% planned-route-miles reduction lacks baseline miles or a comparison period.
“Modeled ... as a vehicle-routing problem” identifies the problem type but not the technical work used to solve it.
The change from 120 to 90 miles is not a 40% reduction, and it conflicts with the separate 18% reduction unless the measures differ.
items.because: Thirty miles divided by the original 120 miles is 25%, making the project's core result look unreliable.

items.says: Solving the problem with customer time windows names a constraint but not the solving technique or specific modeling action.
“Raised on-time deliveries by 9%” misstates the change from 84% to 93%.
items.because: The change is nine percentage points, while the relative increase is approximately 10.7%.

items.says: “In simulation” does not state the simulation scope or what counted as an on-time delivery.
items.because: Without the number of simulated days or stops and the timing criterion, the service-level result is harder to judge or reproduce.

items.says: Adding customer time windows repeats the previous bullet's method without distinguishing the additional work behind this result.
The first two routing bullets repeat the distance result instead of separating primary impact from distinct technical evidence.
items.because: Both describe reduced route miles or length, and their differing figures look inconsistent until the measures are explained.

items.says: The analysis and recommendations do not show what analysis was performed or what operational change resulted.
items.because: The reader cannot tell whether the work improved warehouse performance or remained an advisory deliverable.

items.says: The analysis and recommendations provide no measure of the problem, improvement, or scope.
items.because: Without an anchor, the reader cannot judge the analysis's scale or demonstrated value.

items.says: “Made recommendations” is vague, and naming the food bank's leadership does not clarify the work.
“Donations reached the shelves a day sooner” lacks a comparison point.
The passive wording obscures the candidate's actions in mapping intake and removing duplicate steps.
The re-slotting statement shows adoption but not the improvement produced, and “again” is redundant.
Use by the volunteer coordinators does not show how broadly or effectively the guide was applied.
